turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hi Dr. [Name]. Thank you for seeing me. I, um... I guess the main reason I’m here—and it’s a little hard to explain because it’s not like a physical pain or a specific event that happened—but what made me finally make the appointment is that the things that usually make me feel like *me* have just... stopped. 

I’ve always been a very active, highly organized person. I’m an executive administrative assistant, so keeping things running smoothly and staying on top of schedules is literally my livelihood, you know? I usually pride myself on keeping a perfectly clean calendar, color-coded, everything in its proper place, both at work and in my personal life. I usually love that sense of order. But lately, I don't know, it’s like... well, take my photography walks, for instance. I usually go out every single weekend, rain or shine, usually down by the river or through the historic district, just trying to catch the morning light. I have all this gear I usually love setting up, and it centers me. And mentoring the kids—I volunteer with this local youth group, helping teenagers figure out their plans, which is normally the absolute highlight of my week. 

But recently, all of that... the photography, the mentoring, even just the simple satisfaction of keeping that clean calendar... it all started feeling so incredibly flat. Just flat and heavy. Like trying to move through wet concrete. I just stopped initiating them entirely. I’ll wake up on a Saturday and think about grabbing my camera or heading down to the youth center, and this massive weight just sits on my chest, and I just... don't do it. I end up doing nothing at all. It’s just this pervasive, exhausting heaviness where there used to be passion, and it’s been going on long enough now that my calendar is a mess and I haven't taken a single photo in weeks, which is completely unheard of for me. So, I just really needed to figure out why everything feels so empty right now.

turns.doctor_question: I want to make sure I have this right—over these past 11 months, when you've had those high-energy, sleepless stretches where you're redesigning matrices at 3 AM and feeling that electric drive, have you ever experienced any of the following during those times: feeling like your thoughts are racing so fast you can barely keep up, or feeling like you need much less sleep than normal and you're fine with it—like you don't actually feel tired even on just a few hours? turns.patient_response:
The sleep... yes. That is exactly it. It’s actually bizarre when I really stop and think about it, because normally, you know, if I don't get my standard seven or eight hours, I am just a complete zombie the next day at the office. I need my coffee, I need a slow morning, I can barely string a sentence together. 

But during those stretches? It's like my physical body just completely bypasses the biological need for rest. I will have these nights—and this has happened so many times over the last year—where I will maybe, maybe get two or three hours of sleep. Tops. I'll finally force myself to lay down in bed at midnight, just staring at the ceiling, and then by 2:30 or 3 AM, way before dawn, my eyes just snap open. And you would think I'd be absolutely exhausted, right? You'd think I'd be dragging. But I don't feel groggy at all. I don't have that heavy-eyed, sand-in-your-eyes feeling. 

Instead of feeling tired, I feel this intense, immediate readiness. It’s like someone flipped a breaker switch in my chest. I'll literally roll right out of bed in the pitch dark, walk out to the kitchen, and I don't even need to brew coffee because I'm already buzzing. I'll just open up my laptop right there on the kitchen island and I am instantly ready to start answering emails. I'll be firing off replies to our overseas vendors, drafting memos, or I'll pull up the master schedules and just start updating the appointment lists for the senior vice presidents. 

I mean, I'll be sitting there at 3:15 in the morning, just the glow of the screen lighting up the room, cross-referencing three different Outlook calendars, fixing double-bookings, moving meetings around, and I feel completely refreshed. Like I just slept for a week! It’s just... my brain decides that sleep is completely optional, and frankly, just a total waste of time when there are schedules to optimize. So yes, I definitely experience that. Just two or three hours, waking up in the dark, and I'm totally fine with it. I'm ready to conquer the inbox.
